newsitem.title: UK: IRA urged to restore truce to save N.Ireland peace.
newsitem.headline: IRA urged to restore truce to save N.Ireland peace.

text.p: A leading Catholic politician appealed to the IRA on Tuesday to restore its ceasefire to rescue the deteriorating Northern Ireland peace process.

Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), said a statement by jailed Protestant guerrillas that they had lost confidence in peace moves had created a "serious situation, a potential threat to the peace process".

Protestant extremists answered an Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce in September 1994 with their own ceasefire in October. The IRA ended their truce with bombs in London in February but the Protestant guerrilla ceasefire still holds.

Mallon said the IRA could end apprehension over a return to full-scale violence in the British-ruled province by "making clear they are committed to peace and a total ceasefire, and total involvement in the peace process".
"I believe they (the IRA) have it in their power to ensure that the apprehension in the community recedes and that the peace process can be built on," he told reporters.
A politician linked to the pro-British Loyalist guerrillas warned earlier that sectarian bloodshed could return to Northern Ireland if IRA guerrillas launched more attacks.
Northern Ireland has been spared sectarian bloodshed for two years despite the mainland bombing campaign.

"If there is any reaction from Sinn Fein/IRA, then it makes it much more difficult and there is every likeliehood that there could be a return to full-scale conflict," said John White, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party.
Around 1,000 Loyalist and IRA prisoners in Belfast are frustrated that Britain did not respond to the 1994 ceasefires by announcing an amnesty.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said he could understand the frustration felt by prisoners but violence was not the answer.
"I certainly would hope that it is not a return to violence because once violence resumes on their side then I think the scenario becomes very bleak on all sides," he told Irish radio.
White said the Loyalists, who killed hundreds of Roman Catholic nationalists during their campaign, felt Britain had ignored the good faith shown by them in their truce.
"They felt that everything had been done to appease Sinn Fein/IRA and that all concessions that had been granted were towards the nationalist community," White said.

IRA bombs in Britain, and discoveries such as last week's haul of 10 tonnes of explosives in London, have fed fears that despite talk of peace the IRA remains as determined as ever to use force to end British rule.
The IRA's political wing Sinn Fein have been excluded from multi-party talks on the political future of the province -- bogged down in procedural matters -- until the IRA renews its ceasefire.
